summary: A 1974 note describing an approved scheme for connecting host computers to the network through host ports. It deals with the practical question of how a host attaches to the network. Its status is unknown.

eli5.summary: Every computer needs a plug to join the network. This note describes the agreed way to organise those plugs.

questions: how did hosts connect to the arpanet
subtitle: An approved scheme for connecting host computers to the ARPANET through host ports

tldr.problem: As more computers joined the ARPANET, there needed to be a clear, agreed-upon way to connect each host to the network infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 667 documents the approved configuration for BBN, specifying which computers attach to which Interface Message Processors (IMPs) and how they are physically connected.
tldr.outcome: The scheme became effective December 18, 1974, providing a reference implementation for how diverse computer systems could be integrated into the ARPANET.

today: RFC 667 is Unknown status, a configuration record for one ARPANET site from 1974. The specific details are historic, but the principle of documenting host connectivity and numbering schemes remains relevant for network administration.

sections.title: The Host Port Configuration
sections.content:
RFC 667 documents the approved scheme for connecting computers to the ARPANET at BBN. The configuration describes how various PDP-10 and PDP-11 computers connect through Interface Message Processors (IMPs) that form the backbone of the ARPANET. The configuration became effective December 18, 1974.

The document specifies a collection of computers including systems named System A, System B, System C, System D, and special-purpose systems like a speech front end, a line printer terminal, and a packet radio system. Each is assigned a unique host number in both decimal and octal notation.
sections.eli5: This document says which computers connect where on the network, and what number each one gets.

sections.title: Physical Layout and Host Numbers
sections.content:
Most host interfaces are local to BBN, meaning they connect by short cables to their assigned IMPs. The configuration uses host ports for routing: a PDP-11 running a line printer is intentionally assigned a host number that allows a simple program to respond to connection attempts with a message directing users to the correct host number for reaching BBN's main system (System C).

The document includes a detailed diagram showing the interconnection of six computers and specialized systems, their connection points to two IMPs (IMP-50 and IMP-5), and links to a Terminal Interface Processor (TIP) and other network sites. The diagram uses octal notation for addresses, which was standard for PDP systems at the time.
sections.eli5: The document shows a drawing of all the computers and where each one plugs into the network.

sections.title: Host Identification
sections.content:
Each host is assigned a unique identification number in both decimal and octal notation. The system is designed to allow users to find and connect to the correct host using these identifiers. A clever routing convention places a line printer at a host number that can provide directory assistance to new users, guiding them to the correct address for reaching the main system.

This approach to host naming and numbering reflects the early days of the ARPANET, when host addresses were relatively few and simple mapping schemes could be published in RFC documents.
sections.eli5: Each computer gets a number so you know which one you are talking to. One computer was put at a helpful number so it could tell you where to go.
